title: Who does the work, and what it may touch
desc: Settings → Uses: fixed steps, the AI every run, or one of your agents, and the task's own list of apps.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can choose under Settings → Uses whether a Cowork task works as fixed steps, as the AI every run, or as one of your agents, switch it afterwards knowing what that changes, and give the task its own list of apps.

steps.title: Two answers to one question
steps.bodyMd:
Two people at Van Dijk Groep hand over work on the same morning.

Bart, who buys materials, wants a supplier digest at 07:30: read the new mail, group it per supplier, name the order number and the amount. The same work every day, plainly described.

Saskia in HR wants a monthly progress report that sounds like the ones before it and quotes the staff handbook correctly. Her sentence cannot carry all of that, but her HR agent already knows the handbook.

Same Cowork, different answer to one question: **who does the work?** On a task that question lives in one place: **Settings → Uses**, under **How it works**. Beside it sits **Apps it may use**. This chapter is about those two.

steps.title: How it works: three ways
steps.bodyMd:
Open a task, find **Uses** under Settings and choose **Change**. **How it works** offers:

- **Fixed steps**: *the same steps every run, with AI only where something must be written or judged. Fastest and cheapest.* A task made with Set up and test starts this way, where your organisation has fixed steps.
- **The AI works it out every run**: *it reads your sentence and works out the steps on every run. Most flexible, a bit slower.*
- **An agent of yours does it**: *one of your own agents runs it, with its own instructions and apps.* Pick it under **Which agent**.

The Uses row shows the choice while it is closed, for example *No apps · Fixed steps*, or *Your agent 'Inkoop' does it*.

steps.title: Where does each piece come from?
steps.instruction: Saskia's monthly report will run as her HR agent. Match each thing her report needs to where it comes from once the agent does the work.

pairs.left: "A progress report over last month, with the open actions per employee"
pairs.note: What to produce is always yours to say. An agent changes who does the work, never what was asked for.

pairs.left: Every report opens with the same three sentences and never names a salary
pairs.note: Standing rules about voice and limits live in the agent, so they apply to every run without being retyped.

pairs.left: The wording has to follow the staff handbook
pairs.right: A knowledge base attached to the agent
pairs.note: Something the run must look things up in is knowledge, and knowledge is attached to the agent, not to the task.

pairs.left: The run has to read last month's meeting notes
pairs.right: An app the agent is connected to
pairs.note: Reaching out to something is an app. An agent brings the apps it is connected to, which is what How it works says: its own instructions and apps.

pairs.left: Afterwards she wants to ask follow-up questions about this month's report
pairs.note: An agent's run also writes its result into one chat thread that the task keeps using, so she can talk about it there.

steps.question: Bart's digest has run as his purchasing agent every weekday for two weeks. He opens that agent's chat. What does he find?

choices.label: One thread the task keeps using, with each run's result written into it; every run also reached his notifications and the task's History.
A separate new thread for every run, because each run is its own conversation.
choices.feedback: The task remembers the thread its first agent run opened and keeps writing into that one, so the series reads as one conversation.

choices.label: Nothing: with an agent, results only go to the agent's chat and no longer to notifications.
choices.feedback: Nothing is taken away. The notification and the task's own History still hold every run; the agent's thread is an extra copy you can talk in.

steps.explanation: An agent task keeps one thread of its own. That is a practical reason to choose an agent even for simple work: the results collect somewhere you can question them.

steps.title: Two kinds of remembering
steps.bodyMd:
Do not mix these up.

- **What it remembers**, under the task's **Uses**: what this task keeps from one run to the next. You can read it there, and **Clear what it remembers** so the next run starts fresh.
- **The agent's Memory**, switched on in the agent's own settings: when it is on and the agent does a Cowork task, every run of that task is given the things earlier runs already covered, each with the date, and told to skip them unless something changed. A new agent has it off.

For a daily digest that is the difference between "here are the five suppliers again" and "one of the five moved".

steps.title: Handing a task you already have to an agent
steps.instruction: Bart's supplier digest runs as fixed steps. From tomorrow he wants his purchasing agent to do it. Put his moves in the order the screen allows.

items.label: Open the digest from Your tasks
Under Settings, choose Change on the Uses row
Under How it works choose An agent of yours does it, then the agent under Which agent
Save: the note warns that saving takes the fixed steps off
Press Run for real now to see the first agent run land

sim.feedback: Everything about one task is changed on that task, in its Settings, and nothing is written until you save. Going back is the same path: choose Fixed steps again, and Cowork makes and tests new steps that you approve.

steps.title: What you give up when an agent does it
steps.bodyMd:
Switching a task with fixed steps to an agent (or to the AI every run) is a trade, and the screen says so before you save: *Saving takes its fixed steps off: from then on the task is worked out again on every run.*

With the steps go two other things:

- **Ask me**, under Sends to, no longer applies: *This applies to fixed steps. Here the AI or your agent does the task and tells you afterwards what it did.*
- **Steps** shows what the agent did last time, instead of the same steps every run.

So for work that sends messages to other people, fixed steps keep you in the loop; an agent brings knowledge and a thread, and reports afterwards.

steps.question: Saskia's report goes to her and the HR manager, with Show me each message first. She switches How it works to her HR agent and saves. What happens to the message for the HR manager from now on?

choices.label: The Ask me choice no longer applies: the agent does the task and tells her afterwards what it did.
It still waits for her under Needs you, because she chose Show me each message first.
choices.feedback: That is what the earlier choice suggests, but it belongs to fixed steps. The Sends to row says so once the agent does the task.

choices.label: Nothing can be sent at all any more, because agents may only write.
choices.feedback: An agent brings its own connected apps and can use them. What changes is that it does not stop to ask first.

steps.explanation: Fixed steps are what makes asking before each message possible. Keep them for work that reaches other people, or keep the agent's job to drafting.

steps.title: Apps it may use
steps.bodyMd:
Under **Uses** the task's apps sit as chips you switch on or off.

- **No list of its own**: how a task without chosen apps starts. *It uses the apps that are on for you.*
- **Its own list**: the moment you switch one chip off or on. *It only uses the apps that are on here.*
- **All off**: the Uses row reads **No apps**. That is an answer, not a blank: this task may use none.

On a task with fixed steps, other apps means **Save and test**: the steps are made again for those apps, tested, and approved by you.

One rule sits above all of it: if your organisation's **Admin rules** list the apps tasks may use without asking, other apps are left out of every run, whoever does the work.

steps.question: Saskia's report should only reason over the text it is given, so under Uses she switches every app chip off and saves. The row now reads No apps. What has she told Cowork?

choices.label: That this task may use no apps at all, on every run, until she switches one on again.
Nothing: an empty list counts as no choice, so the task falls back to the apps that are on for her.
choices.feedback: Those are two different states. No list of its own is how a task starts; switching every chip off is a list with nothing in it, and the run honours it.

choices.label: That the task may use every app, since a filter with nothing in it filters nothing out.
choices.feedback: The chips are what it may use: only what is on is available to the run. With nothing on, nothing is.

steps.explanation: Empty and absent are different answers. Absent means the apps that are on for you; empty means none, the strictest thing you can say about a task.

steps.title: An agent of yours does it is not offered. Why?
steps.bodyMd:
The choice is only listed when there is an agent to pick, so its absence has causes rather than being a fault.

- **No agents to offer you.** Nothing to choose.
- **Your role may not manage agents.** The list behind the choice is read with the permission that lets someone build agents: Organisation Admin, Agent Admin and Agent Editor have it, a Member does not.
- **The feature is not on for your account.** A save is refused with *Running Cowork items as an agent is not enabled for this account*.
- **You may not use that agent.** A task may run as your own agent, or as a published agent of your organisation that you may chat with; anything else is refused with *Agent not found or not available to you*.

None of this stops the task. Fixed steps or the AI every run still work.

steps.title: Give one task its own list of apps
steps.instruction: Open Cowork and open a task of your own from Your tasks, or make one with a one-line sentence first. Under Settings, choose Change on the Uses row, switch at least one app chip off under Apps it may use, and save (on a task with fixed steps that is Save and test). We then check that the task is in your own list; the Uses row, which now names the task's own apps, is your proof.

steps.title: What breaks once an agent is in the picture
steps.bodyMd:
An agent task has failure modes a fixed-steps task does not, and they all surface the same way: the task reads **Failed** and a card under **Needs you** says what happened.

- **The agent was deleted.** Every task pointing at it fails on its next run.
- **You may no longer use it.** Access is checked again at every run: an agent that was unpublished, or moved out of your groups, stops the task.
- **The feature was switched off** for your organisation.
- **A sign-in ran out.** With an agent, the broken connection may be one the agent reaches for rather than one your sentence mentions. **Sign in again** opens Settings → Connections.

A repeating task keeps its schedule after any of these; the next run tries again.

steps.question: Saskia's monthly report ran as an agent a colleague has since deleted. This morning it failed. What is the fix?

choices.label: Read the card, then under Settings → Uses choose another agent or another way of working, save, and press Run for real now.
Rewrite the sentence under What; a failed run means the sentence was too vague.
choices.feedback: Her sentence never got a chance. The run stopped because the agent it was told to use is gone. Read the card before you rewrite anything.

choices.label: Nothing: the task picks the next available agent on its own.
choices.feedback: Cowork never chooses an agent for you. Who does the work is changed under Uses, by you.

steps.explanation: A missing agent, an agent you may no longer use or a switched-off feature are all problems with who does the work, and every one of them is repaired under Settings → Uses, not in the sentence.

steps.title: Your turn: decide who does the work
steps.instruction: Take one piece of work you would hand over this month, yours or one of the Van Dijk Groep examples. Write four short lines: (1) the sentence for the task; (2) Fixed steps, The AI works it out every run, or An agent of yours does it, and why, in the terms of this lesson (the same work every time, knowledge or a thread an agent brings, asking before messages to others); (3) its apps: no list of its own, its own list (name the apps), or none at all, and why; (4) the one thing you will check on the task after its first run to know the choice was right.
steps.placeholder: e.g. (1) Every weekday at 07:30, summarise new supplier mail in Outlook per supplier with order number, amount and reply-by date, and send it to me. (2) Fixed steps, because… (3) Its own list: only Outlook, because… (4) After the first run I open…

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Choose who does the work on purpose**, under Settings → Uses → How it works. Fixed steps for the same work every time, and for asking before messages to others; the AI every run for work that changes shape; an agent for its instructions, knowledge, apps and one thread where results collect.
- **Say what a task may reach**: no list of its own, its own list, or no apps at all. Your organisation's Admin rules sit above every task.
- **Repair who, not what.** A deleted agent, an agent you may no longer use or a switched-off feature is fixed under Uses, then proved with Run for real now.

And if the agent choice is missing: that is a role or a feature, not a fault. The task still runs.

ex-cowork-run-as-agent-decide.title: Choosing who does the work, and the reach
ex-cowork-run-as-agent-decide.task: Write four lines about one real task: the sentence; Fixed steps, the AI every run, or an agent, with the reason; which apps state the task should be in (no list of its own, its own list with the apps named, or none) and why; and the one thing to check on the task after its first run.
criteria: The sentence says what must be produced and when, not just a topic.

The choice of how it works is justified with something real: the same work every time or asking before messages to others (fixed steps), work that changes shape (the AI every run), or the instructions, knowledge, apps or one continuing thread an agent brings.
The apps answer names one of the three states (no list of its own, its own list with the apps named, or none) and says why that state fits the work.
The check after the first run points at something the task really shows: its latest result, History → Runs, Steps, a card under Needs you, or the agent's thread.
ex-cowork-run-as-agent-decide.guidance: Pass a concrete, honest answer even if short. Do not pass: a sentence that is only a subject line; 'an agent is smarter' or any reason that is not one of the things above; an apps answer that leaves the state ambiguous ('restrict the apps'); a claim that an agent still asks before every message; or a check that cannot be seen on the task, such as a cost figure on the task or a colleague's view of it.

practiceTopic.title: Cowork: who does the work, and what a task may use
practiceTopic.summary: How Settings → Uses → How it works decides between fixed steps, the AI every run and one of your agents, and how a task's own list of apps decides what a run may use.
facts: How it works, under a task's Settings → Uses, offers 'Fixed steps', 'The AI works it out every run' and 'An agent of yours does it' (then 'Which agent').
Switching a task with fixed steps to the AI or an agent takes its fixed steps off; the screen warns 'Saving takes its fixed steps off' before the save.
The Ask me choice under Sends to applies to fixed steps only; for the AI or an agent the row says the AI or the agent does the task and tells you afterwards what it did.
An agent run writes its result into one chat thread of that agent that the task keeps using, and also reaches the notifications and the task's History.
Apps it may use: a task without its own list uses the apps that are on for you; switching a chip gives it its own list; all chips off reads 'No apps' and means it may use none.
The agent choice is only offered when there are agents to pick; the list needs the permission to manage agents (Organisation Admin, Agent Admin, Agent Editor), which a Member does not have.

A task may run as your own agent or a published agent of your organisation that you may chat with; otherwise the save is refused with 'Agent not found or not available to you', and without the feature with 'Running Cowork items as an agent is not enabled for this account'.

If the agent's Memory is on, each run of the same task is given what earlier runs already covered, with dates, and told to skip it unless something changed; a task's own 'What it remembers' under Uses can be cleared so the next run starts fresh.

actionChecks.label: A Cowork task with its own list of apps
actionChecks.hint: Open a task, choose Change on Settings → Uses, switch at least one app chip off under 'Apps it may use', and save. The Uses row then names the task's own apps.

endpoints.returns: { schedules: [...], maxSchedules } — rows scoped to the signed-in user, each with id, userId (owner), title, enabledApps (array of app ids, or null when the task has no list of its own) and agentId

criteria.label: A Cowork task of your own exists
criteria.hint: Open Cowork and make one with a one-line sentence if Your tasks is empty. The task's own list of apps is saved inside the task, where this check cannot look: the Uses row on the task is your proof.
criteria.rule: GET /api/cowork → schedules[] holds a row whose userId is the learner (enabledApps itself is not readable by the runtime)
